input.rationale: Open a third investigation in a different mechanism (client contracts and authority transitions): the Node wrapper's proposal channel. The target's own comment at node.go:409-411 calls the channel reset 'not very sound and likely has bugs', and applying a configuration change that adds the node back does not appear to restore it, so a draft probe was written and run natively. The native run blocked the proposal after the re-add, but it also showed that the probe's readings are taken before the node's run loop has processed a Step, so the observation cannot yet separate the two competing causes; this update records the lead, the sources, the behaviour, the inconclusive native run and the discriminator instead of claiming a defect.

investigations.question: Does the Node wrapper let an application propose again through a node that was removed from the configuration and then added back while the leadership and term are unchanged?
investigations.hypothesis: node.run sets propc to nil when an applied configuration change removes the local node (okBefore && !okAfter and the node is in neither Voters nor VotersOutgoing) and restores it only in the leadership-change branch when a leader is known; applying the change that adds the node back takes the okBefore=false path, so nothing restores the channel. Node.Propose then selects on the nil channel and returns only through the caller's context or the node's done channel, so the re-added member cannot propose until a leadership change occurs.
investigations.discriminator: Whether Propose returns nil for the same application sequence when the node's run loop has demonstrably processed the removal and the re-add (member true, known leader unchanged), and whether a deliberate leadership change makes it return nil again in the same run.

knowledge.statement: node.run sets its proposal channel to nil when an applied configuration change removes the local node from Progress and that node appears in neither cs.Voters nor cs.VotersOutgoing, and restores the channel from n.propc only in the branch that reacts to a change of r.lead with a leader known; applying a change that adds the node back does not restore the channel.
knowledge.conditions: Node wrapper (node.run) driven through ApplyConfChange; the removal is applied while the node is in Progress and the addition is applied while it is not.

knowledge.statement: With the proposal channel nil - either because the node was removed or because no leader is known - Node.Propose sends into a nil channel inside a select that also watches the caller's context and the node's done channel, so the call blocks until one of those fires and then returns ctx.Err() or ErrStopped.

interpretations.rationale: Source account: node.run closes the proposal channel when an applied configuration change removes the local node from the configuration (the guard requires that the node was in Progress before, that it is not in Progress afterwards, and that it appears in neither the incoming nor the outgoing voter list), and the only place that re-opens it is the branch that reacts to a leadership change with a leader known. A node added back by a later change takes the okBefore=false path in that same case, so the channel is left closed while the leader and term stay the same; Node.Propose then selects on a nil channel and can only return through the caller's context or the node's done channel. The draft probe assurance_node_proposal_test.go drives a wrapped node 2 against a bare leader 1, removes and re-adds node 2 through the real propose/apply path, and compares Propose before the removal, after the re-add, and after a leadership change. The native run already shows the blocked proposal (Propose returned context deadline exceeded after the re-add, with the node registered again as a member and still knowing leader 1, and the leader's last index did not advance), but it is not yet admissible evidence: the probe read node 2's status immediately after delivering a message to it, and Node.Step only hands the message to the run loop, so the same run's control observation saw no leader yet and the witness cannot be separated from the competing explanation that the channel was closed because no leader was known at that moment. The next action is to make the probe wait for the observable transition (member and known leader as seen by the reader) before each observation and to keep the leadership-change control, which would let the two explanations be distinguished; no defect is claimed until then.
counterevidence: The Node.Propose documentation states that proposals can be lost without notice and that ensuring retries is the caller's job (node.go:138-140), so a blocked or failed proposal on a re-added node overlaps with behaviour callers are warned about; the specific claim to test is the permanent unavailability of the channel while the node is a member and a leader is known.

The native run's control was taken before node 2 had observed any leader, and with no leader known the channel is nil by the same design (the run loop closes it in the lead-change branch), so the observed block in that run does not by itself identify the removal as the cause.
limitations: Only a native draft run exists so far; there is no retained receipt for this probe, and the probe's own sampling must be corrected before an execution would be meaningful.
The harness drives a wrapped node against a bare raft rather than two application-driven nodes, so the wrapper's asynchronous ready/advance contract is exercised on one side only.

interpretations.rationale: The source account is that a leader takes on a duty when it postpones a received ReadIndex request: pendingReadIndexMessages holds requests that cannot yet be answered because no entry of the leader's term is committed, and they are released when the term's first commit is observed (raft.go:1550-1554 calls releasePendingReadIndexMessages immediately before bcastAppend under the comment 'committed index has progressed for the term, so it is safe to respond to pending read index requests'). The same enabling change of state - raftLog.committed advancing to an entry of the leader's term - is also produced inside switchToConfig, which calls r.maybeCommit() and, on success, only calls bcastAppend (raft.go:2013-2028). Applying a committed configuration change is a legal producer of that path: applyConfChange -> switchToConfig is invoked by the application whenever a configuration change is observed in Ready.CommittedEntries. When the applied change makes ProgressTracker.Committed() exceed raftLog.committed (removing a voter that is unreachable, or leaving a joint configuration whose outgoing half contains such a voter) and the entry at the resulting index carries the leader's term, the commit is performed with the postponed request still unreleased. Because the request was stored in pendingReadIndexMessages and not in readOnly.unconfirmedReads, no later heartbeat can carry its context, so the duty is not discharged by the periodic heartbeat round: the received request yields no ReadState for a local read and no MsgReadIndexResp for a forwarded one until an unrelated entry is committed (which again goes through the MsgAppResp path) or the client retries. The defect is therefore a lost duty on one of two enabling paths, scoped to a bounded interval: from the postponed request until the next commit outside switchToConfig. The returned index remains safe whenever the request is eventually released, because the recorded index is taken from raftLog.committed at release time and raftLog.committed never decreases; the defect is a bounded-liveness (unanswered request) issue, not a stale-read safety violation. A native draft probe of both variants (removing an unreachable voter, and leaving a joint configuration) reproduced the observable sequence: the leader postponed the request (pending_reads=1, committed_entry_term 1, leader term 2), then applying the committed change advanced committed 10 -> 11 with committed_entry_term 2 == leader term while pending_reads stayed 1, no ReadState was produced, the delayed acknowledgement of the previous configuration (match_3=11) did not release it, a heartbeat round carried no read context (heartbeat_ctx_len 0) and did not release it, and only an unrelated proposal committed by the new configuration released the request (read_states 1, request ctx A, index 12 - the later commit index, i.e. answered late rather than answered wrong). The formal execution of this harness is requested with this update; the retained receipt is needed before this account can be treated as an executed comparison.
counterevidence: The Node.ReadIndex contract states that read index requests can be lost without notice and that ensuring retries is the caller's job (node.go:218-224), so a client that retries is not permanently blocked; the observation is a delayed or lost answer of an otherwise admissible request, not a permanent outage.

The library documents that an application may report applied progress before it has finished applying the entries of the previous Ready (node.go:166-178) and fixes no ordering between that evidence and the ApplyConfChange call for a change it has observed (node.go:179-187); the reachable prefix therefore relies on that documented latitude, and an application that calls ApplyConfChange before reporting progress past the change does not hit this path.
limitations: The scenario requires the applied configuration change to be the one that first makes a current-term entry committable; if the leader had already committed any entry of its term, later reads are not postponed (committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is true) and this path is not taken.

interpretations.rationale: The source account: tracker.IsSingleton (tracker/tracker.go:158-162) is a size test - one member in Voters[0] and none in Voters[1] - and its doc comment asserts that this member is the leader, but nothing compares it with the local node id. stepLeader's MsgReadIndex case (raft.go:1354-1361) takes that test as sufficient authority to answer immediately from r.raftLog.committed, for a local request by appending a ReadState and for a forwarded request by sending MsgReadIndexResp, without any heartbeat or readOnly round. The library reaches this state legitimately: applying a committed configuration change that removes the local node while it is leading leaves it leading unless Config.StepDownOnRemoval is set (raft.go:1985-2012 with the documented default false at raft.go:282-287), and its tracker then holds a configuration whose only voter is another node. The same library refuses new proposals from exactly this node (raft.go:1294-1303: 'If we are not currently a member of the range (i.e. this node was removed from the configuration while serving as leader), drop any new proposals'), so the responsibility for the removed leader's behaviour is taken up on the write path and left open on the read path. The consequence is a safety claim, not a progress claim: ReadOnlySafe is documented as achieving linearizability by communicating with the quorum (raft.go:233-244) and ReadIndex promises that work issued before the request can be served once the application has advanced past the returned index (node.go:218-224, README.md:27-32). A client that issues its read through the removed leader - a node that still reports itself as the leader - is handed an index that is below entries already committed by the actual leader of that configuration, so the state it is licensed to serve may miss a write that completed before the read began, and retrying at the same node reproduces the same answer instead of repairing it. The draft probe exercises both halves: it observes the removed leader (config voters=(2), singleton true, is_voter false, still StateLeader) answering MsgReadIndex with read index 2 while the actual leader had already committed index 4, emitting no message at all, and it observes the same request answered by the actual leader with an index that covers its commit index; three later heartbeat intervals produce no reply and the removed leader repeats the same stale index. The formal execution of this harness is requested with this update, so this remains a source-grounded account until its receipt exists.
counterevidence: A client is expected to direct linearizable reads at the current leader; reading through a node that was removed is a client-side premise. The library cannot detect staleness in general: a leader that was removed by a configuration change it has already applied, or one partitioned away, also answers old-term requests until it hears a higher term.

What makes this case the library's responsibility rather than the client's is narrower: the shortcut is taken from the local tracker, which already establishes that the only voter is another node, and the library refuses proposals from that same node; without the shortcut the read would need a quorum acknowledgement from the current configuration, and the removed leader cannot obtain one once the actual leader has moved to a higher term (its heartbeat is ignored or answered with a higher term).
limitations: The scenario requires the application to apply a committed configuration change that removes the leading node while Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false; applications that set that option, or that stop the removed node, do not reach it.

The removed leader remains at its old term only while nothing from the current configuration carries a higher term to it; with CheckQuorum or PreVote enabled the current leader answers the stale heartbeat with its higher term and the removed leader steps down, which bounds the window but does not remove the stale answers issued before that.

result.summary: Opened a third investigation in a different mechanism - the Node wrapper's proposal channel - and recorded its current state rather than a claim. The target's own comment at node.go:409-411 calls the proposal-channel reset 'not very sound and likely has bugs', and reading the code shows the channel is closed when an applied change removes the local node (the guard requires it was in Progress before, is not after, and is in neither voter list) while the only re-opening site is the leadership-change branch with a leader known, so a change that adds the node back takes the okBefore=false path and leaves the channel closed. Recorded sources for the guard, the restore branch, the nil-channel select in Node.Propose and Propose's 'proposals can be lost' documentation, plus two behaviours (the close/restore mechanism; Propose blocking on a nil channel until the caller's context or the node's done channel fires). A draft probe (assurance_node_proposal_test.go) drives a wrapped node against a bare leader, removes and re-adds that node through the real propose/apply path, and compares Propose before the removal, after the re-add and after a leadership change; the native run showed the blocked proposal after the re-add (context deadline exceeded while the node was a member again and still knew leader 1, with the leader's index unchanged) but the run is not admissible: the probe read the node's status immediately after delivering a message, and Node.Step only hands the message to the run loop, so the same run's control saw no leader yet and the block cannot be separated from the competing explanation that the channel was closed for lack of a known leader. The interpretation is therefore unresolved with defect_claim unresolved, keeping that counterevidence and the sampling flaw as limitations; the next action is to make the probe wait for the observable member/leader transition before each observation and keep the leadership-change control, after which an execution can be requested.

A leader whose removal the application applied (StepDownOnRemoval false) therefore keeps answering reads immediately with its own, frozen commit index, even though the library knows from its own tracker that the single voter is another node; the write path guards exactly this case, the read path does not.
history.discriminator: Whether a node in StateLeader whose configuration contains exactly one other voter answers MsgReadIndex with no outgoing heartbeat and no readOnly activity, and whether the returned index is below the commit index of the node that is the actual leader of that configuration.

history.question: What does raft do with a ReadIndex request that reaches a node which is no longer a voter of its own configuration, and is the outcome safe - either the request is answered with a current index, or it is refused and retried elsewhere?

investigations.question: Does the Node wrapper let an application propose again through a node that was removed from the configuration and then added back while the leadership and term are unchanged?
investigations.hypothesis: node.run sets propc to nil when an applied configuration change removes the local node (okBefore && !okAfter and the node is in neither Voters nor VotersOutgoing) and restores it only in the leadership-change branch when a leader is known; applying the change that adds the node back takes the okBefore=false path, so nothing restores the channel. Node.Propose then selects on the nil channel and returns only through the caller's context or the node's done channel, so the re-added member cannot propose until a leadership change occurs.
investigations.discriminator: Whether Propose returns nil for the same application sequence when the node's run loop has demonstrably processed the removal and the re-add (member true, known leader unchanged), and whether a deliberate leadership change makes it return nil again in the same run.

knowledge.statement: A leader that receives MsgReadIndex postpones the request (appends it to r.pendingReadIndexMessages and returns without answering) exactly when its current configuration is not a singleton and r.committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is false, i.e. when the entry at its committed index was issued by an earlier term.
knowledge.conditions: Local raft instance in StateLeader; message type MsgReadIndex; configuration not a singleton (tracker.IsSingleton() false).

knowledge.statement: Postponed ReadIndex requests are released only from the MsgAppResp success path when r.maybeCommit() reports that the commit index advanced to an entry of the leader's term; the helper refuses to release them when committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is false.
knowledge.conditions: StateLeader; MsgAppResp handling for which pr.MaybeUpdate or the probe-recovery condition is true; releasePendingReadIndexMessages is the only consumer of pendingReadIndexMessages.

knowledge.statement: switchToConfig is a second code path on which a leader can perform the term's first commit: when the configuration returned by the conforming changer raises ProgressTracker.Committed() above raftLog.committed and the entry at that index carries the leader's current term, it calls r.maybeCommit() and, on success, only broadcasts appends; it does not release pendingReadIndexMessages.
knowledge.conditions: StateLeader with a non-empty voter set; called from applyConfChange (application applies a committed configuration change) with the leader's Progress values already reflecting quorum-level acknowledgement of a current-term entry.

knowledge.statement: A postponed request is not part of readOnly.unconfirmedReads, so readOnly.heartbeatCtx() returns nil, outgoing heartbeats carry no read context, and the MsgHeartbeatResp handler returns early on an empty context: a periodic heartbeat round cannot release a postponed request.
knowledge.conditions: ReadOnlySafe; pendingReadIndexMessages non-empty while readOnly.unconfirmedReads is empty.

knowledge.statement: The library permits an application to report applied progress (Advance / MsgStorageApplyResp) while it is still applying the entries of a previous Ready, and it fixes no ordering between that progress report and the required ApplyConfChange call for a committed configuration change; the campaign gate hasUnappliedConfChanges() reads raftLog.applied only.
knowledge.conditions: Node/RawNode consumer following the documented Ready/Advance contract.

knowledge.statement: ProgressTracker.IsSingleton returns true exactly when Voters[0] has one member and Voters[1] is empty; it never compares the single voter with the local node id, although its doc comment says the single voting member is the leader.
knowledge.conditions: tracker.ProgressTracker of any raft instance, including one that is no longer a member of its configuration.

knowledge.statement: stepLeader answers MsgReadIndex immediately - with a local ReadState for a local request, or with MsgReadIndexResp for a forwarded one - whenever tracker.IsSingleton() is true, using r.raftLog.committed and without sending any heartbeat or consulting readOnly; otherwise it requires committedEntryInCurrentTerm() and a readOnly round.
knowledge.conditions: StateLeader; MsgReadIndex; tracker.IsSingleton() true.

knowledge.statement: When the configuration change that removes the local node is applied while the node is leading, switchToConfig keeps it leading unless Config.StepDownOnRemoval (false by default) is set; the MsgProp path explicitly refuses proposals from a leader that is not in the configuration ('If we are not currently a member of the range ... drop any new proposals') while the MsgReadIndex path has no equivalent guard.
knowledge.conditions: StateLeader; applyConfChange on a committed change whose resulting configuration does not contain the local node; Config.StepDownOnRemoval false (the default).

knowledge.statement: node.run sets its proposal channel to nil when an applied configuration change removes the local node from Progress and that node appears in neither cs.Voters nor cs.VotersOutgoing, and restores the channel from n.propc only in the branch that reacts to a change of r.lead with a leader known; applying a change that adds the node back does not restore the channel.
knowledge.conditions: Node wrapper (node.run) driven through ApplyConfChange; the removal is applied while the node is in Progress and the addition is applied while it is not.

knowledge.statement: With the proposal channel nil - either because the node was removed or because no leader is known - Node.Propose sends into a nil channel inside a select that also watches the caller's context and the node's done channel, so the call blocks until one of those fires and then returns ctx.Err() or ErrStopped.
knowledge.conditions: Node.Propose/stepWait with the run loop's propc variable nil.

interpretations.rationale: The source account is that a leader takes on a duty when it postpones a received ReadIndex request: pendingReadIndexMessages holds requests that cannot yet be answered because no entry of the leader's term is committed, and they are released when the term's first commit is observed (raft.go:1550-1554 calls releasePendingReadIndexMessages immediately before bcastAppend under the comment 'committed index has progressed for the term, so it is safe to respond to pending read index requests'). The same enabling change of state - raftLog.committed advancing to an entry of the leader's term - is also produced inside switchToConfig, which calls r.maybeCommit() and, on success, only calls bcastAppend (raft.go:2013-2028). Applying a committed configuration change is a legal producer of that path: applyConfChange -> switchToConfig is invoked by the application whenever a configuration change is observed in Ready.CommittedEntries. When the applied change makes ProgressTracker.Committed() exceed raftLog.committed (removing a voter that is unreachable, or leaving a joint configuration whose outgoing half contains such a voter) and the entry at the resulting index carries the leader's term, the commit is performed with the postponed request still unreleased. Because the request was stored in pendingReadIndexMessages and not in readOnly.unconfirmedReads, no later heartbeat can carry its context, so the duty is not discharged by the periodic heartbeat round: the received request yields no ReadState for a local read and no MsgReadIndexResp for a forwarded one until an unrelated entry is committed (which again goes through the MsgAppResp path) or the client retries. The defect is therefore a lost duty on one of two enabling paths, scoped to a bounded interval: from the postponed request until the next commit outside switchToConfig. The returned index remains safe whenever the request is eventually released, because the recorded index is taken from raftLog.committed at release time and raftLog.committed never decreases; the defect is a bounded-liveness (unanswered request) issue, not a stale-read safety violation. A native draft probe of both variants (removing an unreachable voter, and leaving a joint configuration) reproduced the observable sequence: the leader postponed the request (pending_reads=1, committed_entry_term 1, leader term 2), then applying the committed change advanced committed 10 -> 11 with committed_entry_term 2 == leader term while pending_reads stayed 1, no ReadState was produced, the delayed acknowledgement of the previous configuration (match_3=11) did not release it, a heartbeat round carried no read context (heartbeat_ctx_len 0) and did not release it, and only an unrelated proposal committed by the new configuration released the request (read_states 1, request ctx A, index 12 - the later commit index, i.e. answered late rather than answered wrong). The formal execution of this harness is requested with this update; the retained receipt is needed before this account can be treated as an executed comparison.
counterevidence: The Node.ReadIndex contract states that read index requests can be lost without notice and that ensuring retries is the caller's job (node.go:218-224), so a client that retries is not permanently blocked; the observation is a delayed or lost answer of an otherwise admissible request, not a permanent outage.

The library documents that an application may report applied progress before it has finished applying the entries of the previous Ready (node.go:166-178) and fixes no ordering between that evidence and the ApplyConfChange call for a change it has observed (node.go:179-187); the reachable prefix therefore relies on that documented latitude, and an application that calls ApplyConfChange before reporting progress past the change does not hit this path.
limitations: The scenario requires the applied configuration change to be the one that first makes a current-term entry committable; if the leader had already committed any entry of its term, later reads are not postponed (committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is true) and this path is not taken.

interpretations.rationale: The source account: tracker.IsSingleton (tracker/tracker.go:158-162) is a size test - one member in Voters[0] and none in Voters[1] - and its doc comment asserts that this member is the leader, but nothing compares it with the local node id. stepLeader's MsgReadIndex case (raft.go:1354-1361) takes that test as sufficient authority to answer immediately from r.raftLog.committed, for a local request by appending a ReadState and for a forwarded request by sending MsgReadIndexResp, without any heartbeat or readOnly round. The library reaches this state legitimately: applying a committed configuration change that removes the local node while it is leading leaves it leading unless Config.StepDownOnRemoval is set (raft.go:1985-2012 with the documented default false at raft.go:282-287), and its tracker then holds a configuration whose only voter is another node. The same library refuses new proposals from exactly this node (raft.go:1294-1303: 'If we are not currently a member of the range (i.e. this node was removed from the configuration while serving as leader), drop any new proposals'), so the responsibility for the removed leader's behaviour is taken up on the write path and left open on the read path. The consequence is a safety claim, not a progress claim: ReadOnlySafe is documented as achieving linearizability by communicating with the quorum (raft.go:233-244) and ReadIndex promises that work issued before the request can be served once the application has advanced past the returned index (node.go:218-224, README.md:27-32). A client that issues its read through the removed leader - a node that still reports itself as the leader - is handed an index that is below entries already committed by the actual leader of that configuration, so the state it is licensed to serve may miss a write that completed before the read began, and retrying at the same node reproduces the same answer instead of repairing it. The draft probe exercises both halves: it observes the removed leader (config voters=(2), singleton true, is_voter false, still StateLeader) answering MsgReadIndex with read index 2 while the actual leader had already committed index 4, emitting no message at all, and it observes the same request answered by the actual leader with an index that covers its commit index; three later heartbeat intervals produce no reply and the removed leader repeats the same stale index. The formal execution of this harness is requested with this update, so this remains a source-grounded account until its receipt exists.
counterevidence: A client is expected to direct linearizable reads at the current leader; reading through a node that was removed is a client-side premise. The library cannot detect staleness in general: a leader that was removed by a configuration change it has already applied, or one partitioned away, also answers old-term requests until it hears a higher term.

What makes this case the library's responsibility rather than the client's is narrower: the shortcut is taken from the local tracker, which already establishes that the only voter is another node, and the library refuses proposals from that same node; without the shortcut the read would need a quorum acknowledgement from the current configuration, and the removed leader cannot obtain one once the actual leader has moved to a higher term (its heartbeat is ignored or answered with a higher term).
limitations: The scenario requires the application to apply a committed configuration change that removes the leading node while Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false; applications that set that option, or that stop the removed node, do not reach it.

The removed leader remains at its old term only while nothing from the current configuration carries a higher term to it; with CheckQuorum or PreVote enabled the current leader answers the stale heartbeat with its higher term and the removed leader steps down, which bounds the window but does not remove the stale answers issued before that.

Only the declared probe has been run natively so far; the retained receipt for this harness is still outstanding, and no bound is claimed for how long a client that never retries elsewhere stays exposed.

interpretations.rationale: Source account: node.run closes the proposal channel when an applied configuration change removes the local node from the configuration (the guard requires that the node was in Progress before, that it is not in Progress afterwards, and that it appears in neither the incoming nor the outgoing voter list), and the only place that re-opens it is the branch that reacts to a leadership change with a leader known. A node added back by a later change takes the okBefore=false path in that same case, so the channel is left closed while the leader and term stay the same; Node.Propose then selects on a nil channel and can only return through the caller's context or the node's done channel. The draft probe assurance_node_proposal_test.go drives a wrapped node 2 against a bare leader 1, removes and re-adds node 2 through the real propose/apply path, and compares Propose before the removal, after the re-add, and after a leadership change. The native run already shows the blocked proposal (Propose returned context deadline exceeded after the re-add, with the node registered again as a member and still knowing leader 1, and the leader's last index did not advance), but it is not yet admissible evidence: the probe read node 2's status immediately after delivering a message to it, and Node.Step only hands the message to the run loop, so the same run's control observation saw no leader yet and the witness cannot be separated from the competing explanation that the channel was closed because no leader was known at that moment. The next action is to make the probe wait for the observable transition (member and known leader as seen by the reader) before each observation and to keep the leadership-change control, which would let the two explanations be distinguished; no defect is claimed until then.
counterevidence: The Node.Propose documentation states that proposals can be lost without notice and that ensuring retries is the caller's job (node.go:138-140), so a blocked or failed proposal on a re-added node overlaps with behaviour callers are warned about; the specific claim to test is the permanent unavailability of the channel while the node is a member and a leader is known.

The native run's control was taken before node 2 had observed any leader, and with no leader known the channel is nil by the same design (the run loop closes it in the lead-change branch), so the observed block in that run does not by itself identify the removal as the cause.
limitations: Only a native draft run exists so far; there is no retained receipt for this probe, and the probe's own sampling must be corrected before an execution would be meaningful.
The harness drives a wrapped node against a bare raft rather than two application-driven nodes, so the wrapper's asynchronous ready/advance contract is exercised on one side only.

Whether an application is expected to keep proposing through a node that has been removed and re-added is itself part of the question; the library's own comment calls the current mechanism unsound rather than documenting an intended semantics.
